content: Graves' disease is characterized by the presence of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TSH receptor antibodies that target TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells. This interaction leads to excessive production of thyroid hormones. Additionally, immunologically activated fibroblasts in the skin and eyes contribute to the development of dermopathy and ophthalmopathy. While genetic factors play a relatively minor role, the HLA-DR3 allele has been identified as a documented risk factor. Viral or bacterial infections, such as those caused by E. coli or Yersinia enterocolitica, can also act as triggers for hyperthyroidism. This occurs because antibodies generated against these pathogens' cell membranes can cross-react with TSH receptors. This phenomenon, known as the Jod-Basedow effect, is more likely to occur in individuals with pre-existing autonomously functioning thyroid tissue or in patients with endemic goiter who are subsequently treated with iodine. Furthermore, the anti-arrhythmic drug amiodarone, which contains iodine in quantities exceeding the recommended daily allowance, can precipitate hyperthyroidism in susceptible individuals. Clinically, hyperthyroidism presents with a variety of symptoms across multiple organ systems. Thyroid enlargement may be either nodular or diffuse. Gastrointestinal manifestations include weight loss, increased appetite, vomiting, and diarrhea. Neuromuscular symptoms may include nervousness, tremors, psychosis, and hyperreflexia. Dermatological findings include increased sweating, palmar erythema, pigmentation changes, and alopecia. Diagnostic evaluation begins with measuring TSH levels, which are typically suppressed or undetectable in the majority of hyperthyroid cases. This is the primary screening test, as a normal TSH level effectively rules out hyperthyroidism. Serum T3 and T4 levels are elevated in nearly all cases of hyperthyroidism. While iodine-131 uptake studies are not routinely required, they often reveal increased uptake in affected individuals. Additionally, thyroid peroxidase antibody levels are frequently elevated, providing further evidence of autoimmune thyroid dysfunction.
